newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia set for second poll since independence.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia set for second poll since independence.

text.p: Slovenians vote on Sunday in their second general election since independence from former Yugoslavia, with polls showing Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek likely to return to power to head a new coalition government.
More than 1.5 million Slovenians, including ethnic Italians and Hungarians, are eligible to vote for the 24 political parties fielding candidates in the election.
Polls open at 7 a.m. local time (0600 GMT) and close at 7 p.m. (1800 GMT), when first computer projections are expected.

Opinion polls show Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats, credited with establishing a stable democracy and a thriving economy since the last general election in 1992, likely to remain the biggest party in the 90-seat parliament.

Drnovsek, president of former Yugoslavia between 1989 and 1990, has led a shaky coalition of right and leftwing parties over the past four years, but prevented the administration from collapsing on more than one occasion.
The Liberal Democrats, who hold 28 parliamentary seats, rule in coalition with Christian Democrats who have 16, and with cooperation from independents.

The centre-right Social Democrats quit the coalition in 1994 after their leader Janez Jansa was sacked as defence minister. The United List of Social Democrats, the former communists, withdrew from the coalition last January in a row over economic policy.

Slovenia, the northernmost and most ethnically-homogeneous of former Yugoslavia's republics, has made strides under Drnovsek's rule to become one of the most successful economies among Europe's ex-communist states, with an international credit rating ahead of the Czech Republic and Poland.
The country seceded from the Yugoslav federation after a 10-day war in June 1991 in which 64 people were killed.

While inflation has dropped to around 10 percent and annual growth risen consistently over the past four years, unemployment has become the main government bugbear, soaring to more than 13 percent in 1996.

Drnovsek's government gave in to a series of public sector pay strikes this election year, but he has warned labour unions that tough public spending decisions lie ahead to prepare Slovenia for European Union membership.
Drnovsek crowned his term of office in June by signing an association agreement with the EU. Ljubljana hopes to join the Brussels club by the year 2001.

The mountainous state, bordered by Italy, Austria, Hungary and Croatia, has won plaudits for anchoring a stable democracy. No international organisations or human rights groups have deemed it necessary to send observers to Sunday's election.

Stability, and its position so close to the still-volatile Balkan peninsula, have been the reasons behind Slovenia emerging as one of the top candidates in NATO's first bid to include ex-communist states as members.
